• Correct Answer: Black pepper was in immense demand across the Greco-Roman world (referred to in ancient Sanskrit sources as Yavanas) for seasoning and food preservation, earning it the literal Sanskrit epithet 'Yavanapriya' (beloved of the Greeks/Romans).
• Option A is incorrect: Muslin was extensively traded to the West—famed in Roman accounts as 'Ventus Textilis' (woven wind)—and denoted in Sanskrit by terms like 'Karpasa' or 'Dukula', not 'Yavanapriya'.
• Option B is incorrect: Ivory was an important ancient export to Rome (referred to as 'Danta' or 'Gaja-danta'), but it was not known by the term 'Yavanapriya'.
• Option C is incorrect: While Greek slave girls and women were brought to Indian royal courts as bodyguards and performers (often called 'Yavanis'), Indian damsels sent to Greek courts were not termed 'Yavanapriya'.
• Often confused with: 'Yavani', which refers to foreign/Greek women serving as bodyguards, attendants, or cup-bearers in Indian courts (notably referenced in Kalidasa's plays and Arthashastra), rather than trade commodities like pepper.
